issue_context.title: Potential breaking change in socket close behavior in net6 over net5 on Linux
issue_context.body:
It appears that when a NET6 program closes in a non-graceful scenario such as SIG_QUIT, it will modify the SO_LINGER option on its open listening socket. Specifically, it sets SO_LINGER to true, with a timeout of 0 seconds. Kestrel is listening on that socket; we invoke KestrelServerOptions.ListenHandle(...) during startup, and the socket handle is passed in via environment variable - e.g. the listening socket lives longer than the server program.

The code that does that appears to be taking some sort of "abortive" path, as in
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/57bfe474518ab5b7cfe6bf7424a79ce3af9d6657/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SafeSocketHandle.Unix.cs#L264

The code above seemed similar to us between NET5 and NET6, e.g. the behavior wouldn't change, unless the "abortive" had a different value in NET6 for shutdown initiated with SIG_QUIT.

We were able to prove that when the same dotnet program targeting NET5 is shut down using SIG_QUIT, it does not apply any modification to the listening socket, leading us to believe that the "abortive" path in the code above wasn't taken in NET5, but it's taken in NET6.

In our case, the listening socket was passed to the program at start-up time by handle. We expect our program to not modify attributes of this externally provided socket.

This change in behavior between NET5 and NET6 does not appear in the list of breaking changes for NET6 over NET5.
It appears to be a breaking change to us though. 

If this is indeed a breaking change, we'd like it to be documented.
Also, we need a way to prevent .NET runtime from modifying attributes of this socket.

> It appears that when a NET6 program closes in a non-graceful scenario such as SIG_QUIT, it will modify the SO_LINGER option on open listening Sockets.

So, you don't have this behavior with a graceful shutdown?

I wonder if the abortive close is due to the Socket getting disposed from the finalizer thread.
It would help if you can provide a small reproducer.

> In our case, the listening socket was passed to the program at start-up time by handle. We expect our program to not modify attributes of this externally provided socket.

When you create the `SafeSocketHandle`, have you tried using `ownsHandle = false`?

That will cause the close behavior to be skipped:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bab1a1f239325746873d2ae795ea343e7901dbce/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/Socket.cs#L3140-L3141

Is it Kestrel that's listening? Looking at https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/43385, could it be because Kestrel has an outstanding I/O operation (accept) when it disposes the Socket? Kestrel could cancel AcceptAsync with a token before closing the listen socket if that would help. We've avoided it to this point because we wanted to avoid the cost of AcceptAsync registering with the token, but relative to the overall cost of accepting a connection, it's not that much.

I think Kestrel has similar issues with connected sockets. See https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/41074#issuecomment-1145572790 I'm interested on any input you might have there too @tmds.

> Is it Kestrel that's listening?

Kestrel is listening, that's correct. We invoke KestrelServerOptions.ListenHandle(...) during startup, and the socket handle is passed in via environment variable. 

We can't be 100% sure if Kestrel is handling a request during shutdown in all cases: at least one of the affected server applications processes a few hundred requests per second - so there's certainly at least a few requests in flight at shutdown, however another affected server application is not highly loaded and it might potentially be idle at that time.  

> When you create the SafeSocketHandle, have you tried using ownsHandle = false?

We don't use SafeSocketHandle. We pass the handle's parsed ulong directly into KestrelServerOptions.ListenHandle.

> KestrelServerOptions.ListenHandle

This ends up creating a `SafeSocketHandle` that owns the handle here: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/d96a100bddc72606f7417b665428411388b8ac54/src/Servers/Kestrel/Transport.Sockets/src/SocketTransportOptions.cs#L108-L110.

We should change that so the handle is no longer owned.

That will opt-out of the socket closing here:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bab1a1f239325746873d2ae795ea343e7901dbce/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/Socket.cs#L3140-L3141

Though, that closing includes the aborting the on-going operations here:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/bab1a1f239325746873d2ae795ea343e7901dbce/src/libraries/System.Net.Sockets/src/System/Net/Sockets/SafeSocketHandle.Unix.cs#L175-L179

which we still like to happen even when the handle is not owned.
That should cause the `AcceptAsync` to abort.

I think this can work, but the devil may be in the implementation.

Should we transfer this to Kestrel or do you think the fix should some somehow to runtime @tmds? 
I could understand argument that if the `Socket` was created from `descriptor` and does not own it, we should not touch it beyond requested operations. 
I don't know if the Kestrel note about hanging is true for Async operations. AFAIK we had issue only in sync path as we were stuck in kernel call.

Kestrel calls `new SafeSocketHandle((IntPtr)fileHandle.FileHandle, ownsHandle: true)`. I think we're getting what we [ask for](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/Servers/Kestrel/Transport.Sockets/src/SocketTransportOptions.cs#L98-L111). I guess the only ask would be if we set `ownsHandle: false`, could `Socket` still cancel any pending `AcceptAsync` calls when it's disposed? That'd be ideal.


Otherwise, Kestrel is going to have to switch to cancelling its accept loops with a `CancellationToken` instead of just disposing the listen `Socket` just to fix this scenario.

> I guess the only ask would be if we set ownsHandle: false, could Socket still cancel any pending AcceptAsync calls when it's disposed? That'd be ideal.

Yes, I was suggesting this approach in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/70311#issuecomment-1157686760.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/72000 implements it.

review_comments: I think it would be wise to add tests verifying that a non-owned handle will not be closed by Dispose and finalization. (Couldn't find existing ones, maybe just missed them?)
That makes sense. I'll add those.

We do not keep the reference of the original `Socket` instance after this line. Couldn't this lead to an unexpected eager finalization of that instance while `client` and `owner` are still alive?

Otherwise it will be just an ignored failing `close()` syscall in the finalizer, right?

If we're replacing `client` (when `owning` is `true`) the original `Socket` gets:
```
            socket.SafeHandle.SetHandleAsInvalid();
```
so it will no longer `close` the platform socket.

We're cancelling all operations that are performed against the handle here.
If there is another `SafeSocketHandle` for the same raw handle in this process, it may get its operations aborted by this.

For Unix we track the on-going operations performed against the `SafeHandle` in `SocketAsyncContext` so we're only canceling the operations that were performed against that handle.
On Unix we actually don't support different `SafeSocketHandle`s to perform async operations on the same raw handle. `SocketAsyncEngine` holds a map from the raw handle to one `SocketAsyncContext`.
Can we imagine a *sane* user scenario where this could lead to an issue?

So if we don't own the handle we won't attempt to abort ongoing sync operations anymore on `Socket` / `SafeSocketHandle` close? I assume this is not an issue, because in the owning case we are doing it only to prevent an indefinitely blocking `close()` syscall (or a handle leak if we don't close)? Am I following this correctly?
We're not doing it because the function has side-effects which we don't want on a non-owning socket.
